scenarios.title: Which bullet survives
scenarios.situation: You are trimming your resume to one page. You have two bullets competing for the last slot. Bullet A: 'Maintained the deployment pipeline and wrote shell scripts.' Bullet B: 'Cut deploy time from 40 minutes to 6 by rebuilding the pipeline, unblocking 12 engineers.' You can keep only one.
scenarios.prompt: Which bullet should you keep, and why?
choices: Bullet B, because it states a measurable outcome and who benefited, which is what hiring managers screen for
Bullet A, because it lists more technologies and keywords for automated screening
Bullet B, but rewritten to remove the numbers so it sounds less like bragging
Keep both and drop the summary section instead, since more detail is always better
scenarios.why: Hiring managers scan for evidence of impact, not duties. Bullet B names a before/after metric and a beneficiary, which lets the reader infer your skill level without you listing tools. Keyword stuffing helps only if the bullet also proves you used the tool to achieve something.
scenarios.hint: Ask which bullet would still impress if you removed every technology name from it.

scenarios.title: The first offer
scenarios.situation: After three interviews, a company extends an offer: $115,000 base, standard benefits, start in three weeks. The recruiter says the offer expires in 48 hours and asks for your decision. Your research suggests the market range for the role is $120,000-$140,000.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest next move?
choices: Thank them, express enthusiasm, and ask for a few more days plus a conversation about total compensation, citing your market research
Accept immediately, since pushing back risks the offer being rescinded
Reject it outright for being below market and keep interviewing
Accept verbally but keep interviewing, planning to renege if something better appears
scenarios.why: Almost every first offer has room to move, and asking professionally almost never costs you the offer. You need time to evaluate total compensation (bonus, equity, benefits, time off), not just base. Accepting under pressure or reneging later both damage your leverage and reputation.
scenarios.hint: What does the deadline cost them if you ask for three more business days?

scenarios.title: The cold message
scenarios.situation: You want to connect with a senior engineer at a company you admire. You have no mutual contacts. You draft: 'Hi, I'm looking for a new role and saw your company is hiring. Could you refer me? Happy to send my resume.'
scenarios.prompt: How should you improve this outreach?
choices: Lead with something specific you learned from their public work, ask one short question, and make the ask tiny and easy to answer
Send the same message to 50 people, since networking is a numbers game
Attach your resume and a 3-paragraph career summary so they have full context
Wait until you are unemployed so the request feels more urgent and honest
scenarios.why: Cold outreach works when the cost of replying is near zero and you have shown genuine attention first. Referencing their actual work proves you are not mass-blasting, and a single specific question is easy to answer. Attaching a resume to a stranger creates work for them before any relationship exists.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest reply this person could send that would still help you?

scenarios.title: Proof of work
scenarios.situation: You have ten hours a month for personal branding. Option A: polish your LinkedIn headline and post daily motivational quotes. Option B: write one deep technical post per month about a real problem you solved, with code. Option C: collect endorsements for 40 skills.
scenarios.prompt: Which investment best builds a credible professional brand?
choices: Option B, because a public record of solved problems is verifiable proof of competence that compounds over time
Option A, because posting frequency drives profile views, which is the real metric
Option C, because a long skills list passes more automated recruiter filters
None of them; personal branding is vanity and hiring is purely about interviews
scenarios.why: A brand is a promise backed by evidence. One substantive write-up demonstrates how you think, which is exactly what hiring managers and peers evaluate. Frequency without substance and endorsement counts are both cheap signals that experienced reviewers discount heavily.
scenarios.hint: Which option still helps you if nobody likes or shares it?

scenarios.title: Two offers, one clock
scenarios.situation: Company X offers $130,000 with a start date in two weeks and wants an answer Friday. Company Y, which you prefer, is two interview rounds from an offer and moves slowly. You have no other pipeline.
scenarios.prompt: What is the soundest way to handle the timing conflict?
choices: Tell Y you have a competing offer with a Friday deadline and ask if they can accelerate, while asking X for a short extension to decide responsibly
Accept X now and keep interviewing at Y, planning to quit X if Y comes through
Decline X to avoid seeming desperate, betting Y will make an offer
Tell X about Y's slower process to pressure X into raising the offer immediately
scenarios.why: A real competing offer is the strongest legitimate accelerant in hiring, and most companies will compress their process when told honestly. Asking X for a few extra days is normal. Accepting with intent to renege burns a bridge and can get you blacklisted; declining a solid offer on a bet is unforced risk.
scenarios.hint: Which moves keep every option open without misleading anyone?

scenarios.title: The salary-history question
scenarios.situation: In a first-round interview, the recruiter asks: 'What are you currently making?' You know many jurisdictions now restrict employers from asking this, and you also know your current pay is below market.
choices: Decline to share history and redirect to expectations: state the range you are targeting based on market research for this role
Answer honestly with your exact current salary, since honesty is always the best policy
Inflate your current salary so the offer anchors higher
Refuse to answer and lecture the recruiter about labor law
scenarios.why: Disclosing a below-market salary anchors all future numbers to it, which is precisely why many places ban the question. Redirecting to your target range keeps the negotiation anchored to the role's market value instead of your history. Lying about pay is discoverable and a firing offense; lecturing the recruiter poisons the relationship.
scenarios.hint: Which number should the negotiation be anchored to: your past or the role's market?

lessons.title: Career — Core concepts
concepts: Positioning beats pedigree: employers buy outcomes, so frame every role as problems solved and results delivered, with numbers where you have them.
Your brand is your proof: public writing, shipped projects, and talks are verifiable evidence of how you think; endorsements and buzzwords are cheap signals.
Network before you need it: give first (answers, introductions, useful feedback), keep asks tiny, and maintain relationships in good times so they exist in bad ones.
Negotiate total compensation, not just salary: base, bonus, equity, benefits, time off, and flexibility all have value, and the first offer is rarely final.
Interviewing is a skill separate from doing the work: build a bank of STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and rehearse them out loud.
Career capital compounds: rare and valuable skills, a public record, and a trusted network make each subsequent move easier than the last.

example.code:
$ wc -w resume.txt
487 resume.txt
$ grep -oiE 'led|shipped|launched|cut|reduced|saved|automated' resume.txt | sort | uniq -c
      3 led
      2 shipped
      1 reduced
example.walkthrough: A quick audit of your resume: roughly one page per ten years of experience, and every bullet should carry an outcome verb plus a number. If the verb count is low, rewrite duties as results before you apply anywhere.

pitfalls: Common trap: mass-applying with a generic resume; ten tailored applications beat a hundred identical ones.
Common trap: accepting the first offer under a 48-hour deadline without evaluating total compensation.
Common trap: networking only when desperate, which makes every message read as transactional.
Common trap: listing skills with no proof; claims without evidence are filtered out by experienced reviewers.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Build your STAR story bank
labs.objective: Draft five interview-ready STAR stories with quantified results so you never improvise under pressure.
steps: Create star-bank.md with five headings: one per story.
Under each, write Situation and Task in two sentences max.
Write the Action as what YOU did (not the team), starting with a strong verb.
Write the Result with at least one number: time saved, money, scale, or people affected.
Read each story aloud and cut it to under 90 seconds.

checks.hint: Print the file and confirm every story ends with a Result section.
Count your '## ' headings with grep -c to confirm five stories.

labs.title: Total-comp negotiation worksheet
labs.objective: Prepare a one-page worksheet with your market range, walk-away point, and ask script before any offer conversation.
steps: Research the market range for the role from at least two salary sources and note the 25th/50th/75th percentiles.
List every comp component: base, bonus, equity, signing, PTO, remote flexibility, and assign each a value to you.
Write your target number and your walk-away number; keep the walk-away private.
Draft a 3-sentence ask script: gratitude, market data, specific request.
Rehearse the script once out loud, including the pause after you state your number.

checks.hint: Your worksheet file should name an explicit walk-away point.

simulations.title: The lowball offer
simulations.brief: The offer letter is here — 20% below your target, 'take it or leave it, we need an answer by Friday.' You want this job. Decide like a negotiator, not a supplicant.

steps.symptom: Offer: $72k. Your target: $90k. Market data for the role: $85-95k. Deadline: Friday. You want the job.
evidence:
Offer: $72k | your target: $90k
Market range: $85-95k | deadline: Friday
You: want this job
options: Accept immediately — a bird in the hand
Counter with evidence: thank them, anchor at $92k citing the market range and your specific value, and ask what flexibility exists on base, bonus, and start date
Reject outright — the lowball is insulting
Accept but plan to keep job hunting
steps.explain: Negotiation is collaborative problem-solving with numbers: gratitude, a counter anchored in market data (not feelings), and multiple levers (base, bonus, start date, review timeline). 'Take it or leave it' is usually an opening position, and exploding offers are often extendable when asked.

steps.symptom: They moved to $80k: 'This is our max for the band.' The hiring manager privately says the band can flex for exceptional candidates.
evidence:
Offer: $80k, 'max of band'
Hiring manager (off-record): 'bands flex for exceptional hires'
Your leverage: two other processes in final rounds
options: Accept $80k — the band is the band
Use the full picture: restate your value, mention competing processes without bluffing, and propose $88k with a 6-month performance review tied to compensation
Threaten to walk unless they hit $90k
Go around the recruiter to the CEO
steps.explain: Real leverage is real alternatives — mention them honestly, never as a bluff. And the 6-month review clause converts 'we can't' into 'prove it and we will': it gives them a face-saving yes and gives you a contractual second negotiation.

steps.symptom: Final: $86k base, $5k signing bonus, 6-month comp review. Above your walk-away, below your target. Friday is here.
options: Hold out for the full $90k
Accept: it clears your walk-away, the review clause protects the upside, and the role itself is what you wanted — then negotiate hard at month six with evidence
Accept but feel resentful
Ask for the weekend to think, hoping they panic
steps.explain: Negotiation ends with judgment, not victory: $86k clears your walk-away, the signing bonus bridges year one, and the review clause is a scheduled second negotiation. Take the win, document your impact from day one, and come back at month six with receipts.

simulations.debrief: You countered with data, used honest leverage, and closed with a review clause instead of a grudge. Salary negotiation is not combat — it is joint problem-solving where you know your numbers.

simulations.title: Resume vs reality
simulations.brief: You sailed the resume screen — but in the technical interview, your answers do not match your resume's claims. The interviewer notices. Fix the positioning before it becomes a credibility problem.

steps.symptom: Your resume says 'led Kubernetes migration.' The interviewer asks about it; your answers reveal you assisted on one cluster.
evidence:
Resume: 'Led Kubernetes migration'
Reality (your answers): assisted on one cluster
Interviewer: noticeable pause, follow-up questions sharpen
options: Double down — confidence is everything
Correct it in the moment: 'To be precise, I assisted on the migration — I owned the monitoring piece. Let me tell you what I actually did there.'
Deflect to a different topic
Blame the resume writer
steps.explain: The moment you feel the gap, you close it yourself — honestly and specifically. Interviewers forgive junior experience; they do not forgive discovered inflation. 'Let me be precise' followed by real detail rebuilds more credibility than the claim ever built.

steps.symptom: The interview recovered. But the resume still says 'led.' What changes tonight?
evidence: 'Led Kubernetes migration' — still on the resume
options: Leave it — you talked your way through it once
Rewrite every inflated line into precise, verifiable claims: what you owned, what you assisted, what you learned — precision is the whole strategy
Delete the Kubernetes line entirely
Add more impressive verbs to compensate
steps.explain: The resume gets the precision treatment: 'assisted' where you assisted, 'owned' where you owned, numbers where you have them. A resume is a set of claims you must defend live — every line should survive its own interview.

steps.symptom: Resume fixed. A friend asks you to review THEIR resume — it has the same inflation.
evidence: Friend's resume: 'Architected microservices platform' (they configured one service)
options: 'Looks great!' — not your problem
Give them the same medicine, kindly: show them how precision ('configured and monitored X, serving Y requests') actually sounds stronger than the inflated version
Rewrite it for them with bigger claims
Tell them to remove the line
steps.explain: Precision sounds stronger than inflation: specific verbs and real scope are what hiring managers remember. Teaching it to someone else locks in your own lesson — and it is good karma in a small industry.

simulations.debrief: You corrected the record live, rewrote the resume into defensible claims, and taught the principle forward. Careers are built on credibility compounding — one honest correction at a time.

simulations.title: The networking cold email
simulations.brief: You found the hiring manager of your dream role on LinkedIn. No mutual connections. One cold email stands between you and invisibility. Write it right.

steps.symptom: Target: hiring manager, dream role, no warm intro. You have one shot at a cold email that gets opened, read, and answered.
evidence:
Hiring manager, infra team | no mutuals
Their recent post: about the team's migration to event-driven architecture
You: built a small event-driven side project
options: 'Hi, I'm looking for a job. Here's my resume. Can we chat?'
Short, specific, generous: reference their post genuinely, mention your relevant project in one line, ask for 15 minutes of advice — not a job
A long email detailing your life story
Connect with no message and hope
steps.explain: Cold outreach works on specificity and low ask: prove you did homework (their post), offer relevance (your project) in one line, and ask for advice — not employment. 'Can I pick your brain for 15 minutes?' gets answered; 'give me a job' gets archived.

steps.symptom: They replied: 'Happy to chat Thursday.' The call is in two days. How do you prepare?
evidence: Thursday, 15 min | topic: their architecture migration
options: Wing it — it is just a chat
Prepare three thoughtful questions about their migration, one crisp summary of your relevant work, and zero expectation of a referral — then follow up with thanks
Prepare a 10-minute pitch about yourself
Ask for a referral in the first 5 minutes
steps.explain: Networking calls are interviews where curiosity is the product: thoughtful questions about THEIR work, a crisp summary of yours if asked, and no referral ask on call one. The referral comes later — after you have been useful or memorable, not before.

steps.symptom: Great call. They said 'keep in touch.' What does that actually mean, operationally?
evidence: 'Keep in touch!' — Thursday call went well
options: Email them every week with updates
Send a thank-you within 24 hours with one specific takeaway, then follow up quarterly with something genuinely useful (an article, a project update) — 'keep in touch' is a system, not a sentiment
Wait for them to contact you
Immediately ask for the referral
steps.explain: 'Keep in touch' fails without a system: thank-you in 24 hours (with a specific takeaway proving you listened), then light, useful touchpoints quarterly. Networking is farming, not hunting — and farmers keep a calendar.

simulations.debrief: You led with homework instead of hunger, prepared curiosity instead of a pitch, and turned 'keep in touch' into a system. Networking is just being usefully memorable, on a schedule.

simulations.title: Burnout on the job hunt
simulations.brief: 200 applications. 3 callbacks. 0 offers. It is month four, the savings are thinning, and every rejection email feels personal. Respond — to the situation, not just the feelings.

steps.symptom: 200 applications, 3 callbacks (1.5%), 0 offers. Month four. You are starting to dread opening email.
evidence:
200 applied -> 3 callbacks (1.5%) -> 0 offers
Month 4 | savings: thinning
Emotional state: dreading email
options: Double the volume — 400 applications
Diagnose the funnel like an engineer: 1.5% callback means the top of funnel is broken — resume, targeting, or channel — not your worth. Fix the input before scaling the output
Take a month off entirely
Conclude you are unemployable
steps.explain: A 1.5% callback rate is a top-of-funnel problem with a top-of-funnel fix: resume, targeting, or channel — not a verdict on you. Doubling volume on a broken funnel just doubles rejection. Diagnose first, then scale what works.

steps.symptom: Diagnosis: you have been spraying generic applications at senior roles two levels up. The fix is targeting — but targeting feels slower.
evidence:
Pattern: generic resume x 200, mostly senior roles
Actual level: junior/associate
Channel: 100% job boards, 0% referrals
options: Keep spraying — volume will win eventually
Retarget: junior/associate roles, tailored resume per application, 5 quality applications a day, plus 2 networking conversations a week — slower per day, faster per offer
Only apply to dream companies from now on
Pay a resume service $500 and hope
steps.explain: The job hunt is a conversion funnel, and yours was miscalibrated at every stage: wrong level, generic resume, zero referrals. Five tailored applications plus real conversations beat fifty sprays — because referrals convert at 10x job boards and targeting converts at 10x spraying.

steps.symptom: The system is fixed and working — but month five is still hard. How do you sustain yourself?
evidence:
System working, results lagging (hiring takes weeks)
Energy: fragile
options: Grind harder — rest is for the employed
Build the hunt like a job: fixed hours, measurable inputs (not just outcomes), one full day off weekly, exercise, and a weekly review — burnout makes you worse at the thing you need to be good at
Tie your self-worth to the offer count
Isolate until you have an offer
steps.explain: The job hunt is an endurance event run on your own psychology: fixed hours prevent the 14-hour despair spirals, input metrics (applications, conversations) give you wins before offers arrive, and rest is performance equipment. You cannot interview well from burnout.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed the funnel instead of internalizing it, retargeted with precision, and built a sustainable system. The job hunt is a systems problem — and you are the system worth optimizing.

simulations.title: The take-home test
simulations.brief: Final round: a take-home project, 'about 3-4 hours,' unpaid. It is now hour 9 and you see the edge of the scope. The hiring manager 'can't wait to see what you do with it.' Decide your boundaries.

steps.symptom: Hour 9 of a '3-4 hour' take-home. The scope keeps expanding as you see edge cases. You really want this job.
evidence:
Quoted: 3-4 hours | actual: 9+ hours
Scope: expanding | desire for job: high
options: Keep going until it is perfect — the job is worth it
Timebox it: finish a clean, working, documented core in 2 more hours, note the deliberately deferred edge cases in the README, and submit — boundaries are data about you too
Submit the half-done work now with apologies
Withdraw from the process in protest
steps.explain: A take-home that eats 12+ hours is testing your boundaries as much as your code. Timebox, ship a clean core, document the trade-offs explicitly — that README section ('deferred: X, Y because...') demonstrates senior judgment better than a perfect solution does.

steps.symptom: Submitted at hour 11 with documented trade-offs. The hiring manager asks: 'Why didn't you handle the edge cases?'
options: Apologize and offer to do them now, free
'I timeboxed to the quoted scope plus a buffer, and documented what I deferred and why — in production I'd scope the same way. Happy to walk through how I'd handle them.'
'I ran out of time.'
Criticize their take-home design
steps.explain: Defend the boundary as engineering judgment: scoping under constraints IS the skill being tested (or should be). 'How I'd handle them' turns a gap into a demonstration. Never apologize for having a life — frame it as professional scoping.

steps.symptom: You got the job. A friend now faces a 15-hour take-home from another company. What do you tell them?
evidence: Friend: 'This take-home wants 15 hours. Should I do it?'
options: 'Do whatever it takes.'
'Evaluate the company by its hiring process: a 15-hour unpaid take-home signals how they value your time as an employee. Timebox it, or walk — your boundaries are set before you're hired, not after.'
'Just do it, everyone does.'
'Report them.'
steps.explain: The hiring process is the company's culture in preview: how they treat your unpaid time predicts how they treat your paid time. Boundaries set during hiring are the only ones that survive hiring. Teach it forward.

simulations.debrief: You timeboxed with documented trade-offs, defended scoping as a skill, and read the company's culture in its process. Boundaries are not the opposite of ambition — they are how ambition stays sustainable.

consoleSims.title: Track the application pipeline
consoleSims.brief: Run your job hunt like a pipeline: every application is a ticket. Open a P2 ticket for your target application, then assign the seeded INC-9001 to yourself (candidate) as the owner.

tasks.instruction: Create a ticket titled 'Application: Data Analyst role' with priority P2.
tasks.hint: Open New ticket: TITLE='Application: Data Analyst role', PRIORITY=P2.

consoleSims.debrief: Applications are a pipeline: tracked, owned, and staged. What gets ticketed gets followed up.

consoleSims.title: Run the pipeline to offer
consoleSims.brief: The application is moving. Advance INC-9001 to in-progress, log the recruiter screen as a note, then resolve it when the offer lands — with the outcome recorded.

tasks.instruction: Set ticket INC-9001 status to in-progress.
Add a note to INC-9001: 'Recruiter screen scheduled.'
tasks.hint: Add a note on INC-9001 with the exact text.
Resolve INC-9001 with the exact resolution text.

consoleSims.debrief: Every stage logged, every outcome recorded. A pipeline you can review is a pipeline you can improve.

consoleSims.title: Complete your public profile
consoleSims.brief: Recruiters google you. Complete the public profile: set the profile name, the contact email, and submit — an incomplete profile is an incomplete first impression.

tasks.instruction: Set the site_name field to 'My portfolio'.

consoleSims.debrief: Complete profiles get found; complete profiles get contacted. Fill every field — the algorithm and the recruiter both notice.

consoleSims.title: Publish the resume site
consoleSims.brief: Your resume site update is ready. Create a branch feat/resume-site, then open a pull request into main — even personal projects ship through review.

tasks.instruction: Open a pull request titled 'Publish resume site' from feat/resume-site into main.
tasks.hint: Open a PR: TITLE='Publish resume site', BASE=main, HEAD=feat/resume-site.

consoleSims.debrief: Your career artifacts deserve the same rigor as production code: branched, reviewed, merged.

terminalMissions.title: Who is applying
terminalMissions.brief: Careers have owners. Print your username.

terminalMissions.title: Inventory your assets
terminalMissions.brief: A career is a portfolio of assets. List what you have to work with.
terminalMissions.success_message: Assets inventoried. You cannot position what you have not catalogued.

terminalMissions.title: Write your headline
terminalMissions.brief: Every profile needs a one-line headline. Write yours with echo — it must contain "DevSecOps".

checks.hint: Run: echo with your headline (e.g. echo "DevSecOps engineer").

terminalMissions.success_message: Headline written. If you cannot say it in one line, you do not own it yet.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm your home base
terminalMissions.brief: Outreach starts from a known base. Print the hostname.

checks.hint: Run: hostname — confirm your home base.

terminalMissions.success_message: Home base confirmed. Network from somewhere, not nowhere.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm your base of operations
terminalMissions.brief: Print your working directory — the job hunt runs from a known place.
terminalMissions.success_message: Base confirmed. Run the search like an operation, not a hope.

terminalMissions.title: Verify your professional identity
terminalMissions.brief: Print your full identity record — know exactly how you present.

terminalMissions.title: Announce your availability
terminalMissions.brief: Announce you are open to work with echo, then print the platform string for the record — visibility is a strategy.

checks.hint: Run: echo with your announcement (e.g. echo "open to work").

terminalMissions.success_message: Availability announced. The candidate who is visible is the candidate who gets found.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
